input.prompt: Low-poly 3D miniature diorama of a tabletop war game, seen from a high three-quarter angle with a strong tilt-shift effect, so everything looks like a tiny handmade model. Built from simple primitives only: flat-shaded faceted terrain, boxes, cylinders, cones and wedges, with no fine detail and no textures. Palette: terracotta roofs, marble white, weathered bronze, dark olive trees, dusty ochre ground and a hazy blue sky. Setting: an alternate-history Roman frontier fort on a hilltop, where Roman engineers have learned to turn spinning motion into power. In the middle of the fort stands one giant wooden treadwheel, like a Roman treadwheel crane but many times larger, turned by a long line of tiny workers walking inside it. Its axle drives a big spinning bronze flywheel generator that glows faintly at its core. Mounted on the generator housing is a large, clearly readable mechanical drum-counter display showing "1250 W". Spinning bronze drive shafts and chains run from the generator along the walls to the defenses: two ballistae on the corner towers, a rotating bolt thrower and an onager catapult. Enemies climb three dusty roads that wind up the hill toward the gates: a war band of barbarian warriors with round shields, a battering ram under a wooden roof, and a wooden siege tower. Keep the enemies simple, small, blocky and readable, with no gore. All people are tiny, just a few pixels tall; there are no close-up characters and no bicycles. Wide 16:9 game concept art without any user interface. The only text anywhere is the "1250 W" readout; no other letters, numbers, logos or watermarks.

input.prompt: 2D side-view pixel art game scene in a detailed 16-bit style: crisp square pixels and a limited, dark and oily palette of gunmetal grey, soot black, rust brown, olive drab and sickly yellow lamplight, with orange fire glow. An alternate-history 1940s war. A colossal, brutalist super-heavy tank as big as a building, with slab-sided riveted armor and a huge long-barreled gun, grinds across a muddy battlefield of craters, barbed wire and burning wreckage under a smoky sky. Part of its hull is drawn as an x-ray cutaway window that reveals the machine rooms inside, packed with moving parts: crankshafts, flywheels, chains, gears, drive belts, pistons, pressure gauges, glowing valves, leaking oil and puffs of steam and exhaust, all visibly linked to the treads and the turret. This is the one-crew version: inside the cutaway there is a single engine room holding one crude, massive diesel engine with exposed pistons and a heavy flywheel. One long chain and gear train carries its power to everything at once: the drive sprockets of the treads, the turret ring and the shell hoist. Nobody is aboard and no people appear anywhere: the machinery runs on its own. Enemy super-heavy tanks, also huge and menacing, advance from the right, firing. No flags, insignia, national markings, letters or numbers. Wide 16:9 game screen without any user interface.
